cim_eredeti: Ghana Faces Governance Readiness Gap as Artificial Intelligence Deployment Outpaces Oversight
szoveg_eredeti:
Ghana Faces Governance Readiness Gap as Artificial Intelligence Deployment Outpaces Oversight

Artificial intelligence deployment across Ghanaian finance, healthcare, agriculture, digital services, and public administration is expanding more rapidly than the institutional machinery required to supervise its risks, according to a qualitative investigation of the country’s National Innovation System. Researchers Benedict Afful Jr. and Kassim Alabani evaluated Ghana’s institutional environment to determine whether the country possesses the operational capacity, cross-agency coordination, and statutory authority necessary to enforce responsible artificial intelligence standards. Rather than documenting a total absence of governance mechanisms, the empirical findings demonstrate an uneven, system-wide governance readiness gap. While Ghana launched its National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025–2035 on April 24, 2026, and participated in UNESCO’s AI Readiness Assessment Methodology, formal policy ambition has developed ahead of the technical competence, routine advisory channels, and enforcement capabilities of implementing state bodies.

To diagnose why research and policy mechanisms break down, the researchers combined National Innovation Systems theory with Technological Innovation Systems functional analysis and normative governance benchmarks established by UNESCO and the African Union. The investigative framework conceptualized system performance as inherently relational, examining whether universities, commercial enterprises, government ministries, financial institutions, intermediaries, and boundary-spanning professionals effectively exchange knowledge. The authors extended functional analysis beyond industrial output, treating knowledge diffusion, search guidance, resource mobilization, and legitimation as essential governance functions. This framework grounded the study’s central theoretical contribution, termed the Governance Readiness Paradox, which defines a structural condition wherein commercial deployment and high-level strategy accelerate at a pace that continuously outstrips the institutional capacity required to convert technical evidence into enforceable, accountable, and legally sound public oversight.

The empirical research design was rooted in an interpretivist approach that collected qualitative evidence from 32 purposively selected institutional leaders across Ghana’s innovation landscape. The final sample included eight participants from universities and research institutes, six from commercial technology firms and industry, six from government regulatory and policy agencies, four from financial institutions, four from intermediary bodies such as technology hubs and incubators, and four boundary-spanning actors with sustained professional careers bridging multiple sectors. Data collection utilized a three-part qualitative protocol comprising vignette-based scenarios, triadic elicitation, and the Critical Incident Technique. Each semi-structured session lasted 60 to 90 minutes. Vignettes assessed hypothetical responses to simulated real-world dilemmas, including clinical diagnostic failures and discriminatory algorithms, while triadic elicitation prompted participants to compare institutional roles systematically. The Critical Incident Technique gathered detailed first-hand accounts of specific, bounded events where knowledge translation had succeeded, stalled, or failed in practice.

Data were evaluated through reflexive thematic analysis using NVivo software, identifying patterns across participant categories without relying on rigid statistical coder agreement or formal grounded-theory stopping criteria. Coding categories were deductively integrated with Technological Innovation Systems functions and UNESCO and African Union governance pillars: safety and security, transparency, accountability, and inclusion. This thematic structuring established a systemic failure typology consisting of four mutually reinforcing mechanisms: capability failures, connectivity failures, legitimacy failures, and resource failures. Documentary triangulation against publicly available policy frameworks, such as the Data Protection Act 2012 and the National AI Strategy 2025–2035, contextualized the interview narratives. The authors maintained analytic reflexivity and conducted member checking with selected informants to verify that findings accurately reflected the operational landscape while protecting participants from deductive identification.

Universities and research institutes demonstrated substantial epistemic capacity, yet academic respondents reported severe barriers when attempting to transmit technical insights into public policymaking. Participants observed that when research on algorithmic bias was conducted—such as a completed study evaluating automated credit-screening discrimination in domestic financial technology—no formal institutional pipeline existed to translate those empirical findings into regulatory briefs or actionable policy interventions. Triadic comparisons among academic respondents highlighted an institutional disconnect characterized as knowledge without mandate among researchers versus mandate without knowledge among statutory authorities. Furthermore, academic research agendas were found to be predominantly driven by international donor funding. These external grants frequently rewarded technical performance metrics, such as processing velocity and model sophistication, while providing negligible institutional incentives to pursue governance-oriented inquiry, ethical evaluation, or local policy relevance.

Interviews with commercial firms revealed an operational environment where experimental artificial intelligence systems in fintech, health technology, and agritech are adopted far faster than domestic standards for independent audit, public disclosure, and remediation. While enterprises with foreign investors or international accelerator partnerships exhibited greater governance awareness, local firms operated under profound regulatory ambiguity. When presented with a vignette detailing an algorithmic fraud-detection system exhibiting discriminatory bias across a massive user base, industry participants noted that corporate legal counsel routinely advises silence to minimize corporate liability in the absence of explicit statutory disclosure duties. A documented critical incident from the financial sector corroborated this dynamic: an internal corporate audit revealed an automated credit-scoring model that assigned systematically depressed scores to applicants from three northern regions despite repayment records comparable to other applicants. The firm recalibrated the model entirely internally, omitting regulatory notification, affected customer disclosures, or independent remediation.

Government regulatory agencies and ministries exhibited an acute capability-connectivity bottleneck, leaving state entities struggling to operationalize broad policy signals into technical oversight. In response to a vignette requiring a 48-hour parliamentary briefing on an emerging artificial intelligence incident, regulatory officials acknowledged that internal personnel lacked the specialized technical expertise to draft credible assessments independently, while possessing no formal procedures to commission academic assistance on short notice. Although statutory bodies such as the Data Protection Commission and the National Information Technology Agency maintain defined mandates, cross-agency coordination remains fragmented. Critical incident accounts demonstrated that successful knowledge transfer from researchers to state bodies occurred almost exclusively through informal personal connections, temporary academic secondments, or prior individual relationships rather than durable administrative routines.
